problem_statement.text: Differentiate the function.

steps.text: Rewrite the fraction as a power of x.
Differentiate the first term with the power rule.
Differentiate the second term with the power rule.
Add the two derivatives.

why_options.label: Algebraic simplification or factoring error
Solved f(x) = 0 instead of f′(x) = 0
Power rule applied incorrectly to a negative exponent
Forgot to multiply by the inner function's derivative

correct_solution.text: Rewrite the fraction as a power of x.
Differentiate the first term with the power rule.
Power rule: bring the exponent down, then subtract 1 from it (−2 − 1 = −3).
Combine.

rounds.key_lesson: With negative exponents, 'subtract one' moves the exponent further from zero: x^{-2} becomes x^{-3}.
hint_ladder: Which of the four steps uses the power rule on a negative exponent?
What is −2 − 1? Use it as the new exponent of x in the derivative of 5x^(−2).
Write d/dx of x^n = n·x^(n−1) with n = −2, then multiply by 5.

problem_statement.text: Differentiate the function.

Differentiate the outer function with respect to u.

problem_statement.text: Find the critical points of f and classify each one.

steps.text: Differentiate.
Find the critical points by solving f(x) = 0.
Evaluate f at those points.
Classify with the second derivative.
steps.latex: f''(x) = 6 \left(x - 2\right):\quad \text{local max at } x=0;\; \text{local min at } x=3

why_options.label: Incorrect derivative
Mixed up local maximum and local minimum
Algebraic simplification or factoring error
Solved f(x) = 0 instead of f′(x) = 0

correct_solution.text: Differentiate.
Set f′(x) = 0 (not f(x) = 0) and factor.
Critical points
Second-derivative test
correct_solution.latex: \text{local max at } x=1;\; \text{local min at } x=3

rounds.key_lesson: Critical points come from f′(x) = 0. Roots of f(x) are a different question, even when they happen to overlap.
hint_ladder: Critical points are where the derivative is zero. Which equation should be solved?
Check each step against that equation. Expand any factorisation to see if it matches.
If f″ at a point is negative, is the graph concave up or concave down there?

problem_statement.text: Find the absolute maximum of f on the interval.

steps.text: Differentiate.
Solve f′(x) = 0. Both solutions lie in [0, 4].
Evaluate f at the critical points.
The largest value is the absolute maximum.

corrected_step.text: Also compare the endpoints f(0) = -6 and f(4) = 6.

fix_options.text: Also compare the endpoints f(0) = -6 and f(4) = 6.

why_options.label: Forgot to evaluate the interval endpoints
Incorrect evaluation of f at a point
Confused a local extremum with the absolute extremum
Solved f(x) = 0 instead of f′(x) = 0

correct_solution.text: Differentiate.
Critical points: solve f′(x) = 0 and keep those inside [0, 4].
Evaluate f at every critical point AND both endpoints.
Compare all candidate values.

rounds.key_lesson: On a closed interval the absolute extremum can sit at an endpoint. Always evaluate f at the endpoints too.
hint_ladder: On a closed interval, which x-values are candidates for the absolute maximum?
List every candidate: the critical points inside the interval and the two endpoints. Did the attempt check all of them?
Compute f(0) and f(4) yourself and compare them with the values in step 3.
